title: Supplements and Alcohol: Which Are Safe to Mix? A Safety Table
excerpt: Which supplements are risky with alcohol? A safety table covering sedating herbs, serotonin supplements, liver-load products, and the vitamins drinking depletes, with links to every detailed guide.
metaDescription: Which supplements are safe with alcohol? A safety table for sedating herbs, serotonin supplements, liver-load products, and vitamins drinking depletes.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most everyday supplements, like a multivitamin, vitamin C, or magnesium, don't have a dangerous interaction with a normal amount of alcohol. The real risks cluster in four groups: **sedating herbs** (kava, valerian, and similar) that stack with alcohol's drowsiness, **serotonin-adjacent supplements** (St. John's wort, 5-HTP, SAM-e) that mostly matter because of the medications people take alongside them, **liver-load supplements** (kava, high-dose niacin, concentrated green tea extract, and some turmeric and ashwagandha products) that have been linked to liver injury on their own, and a smaller group that affects **blood sugar or bleeding** (berberine, ginkgo). On the other side, heavy drinking drains several vitamins and minerals, so some supplements are less about risk and more about filling gaps.

This page is a hub. It gives you one safety table covering the main supplement classes, explains the mechanism behind each concern in plain words, and links to our detailed page on each supplement.

**The quick rules:** Don't take sedating herbs on nights you drink. If you take a prescription medicine, especially an antidepressant, blood thinner, diabetes drug, or seizure medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement, alcohol or not, because the supplement-drug interaction is often bigger than the supplement-alcohol one. If you drink heavily or have liver disease, avoid supplements with a liver-injury track record and talk to your doctor before starting anything new. No supplement makes it safe to drink more.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide summarizes general research and label guidance about supplements and alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining supplements with alcohol if** you take any prescription medicine, you are pregnant or breastfeeding, you have liver, kidney, or heart disease, you have diabetes, you have a bleeding disorder or upcoming surgery, or you drink heavily on a regular basis. **Get medical help right away if** you notice extreme drowsiness or trouble staying awake, slow or shallow breathing, confusion, a racing heart with fever, agitation, sweating and muscle twitching, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs. In an emergency, call 911. For a possible poisoning, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## Why Supplements and Alcohol Can Clash

Supplements feel harmless because they're sold next to the vitamins, but many of them are biologically active compounds. That's the reason people take them. When you add alcohol, there are four main ways things can go wrong.

1. **Stacked sedation.** Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows brain activity, largely by boosting the calming GABA system and dampening the excitatory glutamate system. Several popular herbs and sleep supplements push in the same direction. Two mild sedatives together can add up to more drowsiness, slower reactions, and worse coordination than either alone. At the extreme end, stacking depressants can slow breathing.
2. **Extra work for the liver.** Your liver breaks down alcohol and most supplements. A few supplements have been linked to liver injury on their own, usually rarely and unpredictably. Alcohol is also hard on the liver. Combining the two doesn't automatically cause harm, but if you're stacking risk factors, this is where it shows up.
3. **Interference with the drugs you already take.** Some supplements change how the liver's drug-processing enzymes (the cytochrome P450 family) work. St. John's wort is the best-known example. It speeds up the breakdown of many prescription drugs, which can make them stop working. Alcohol affects some of the same enzymes, and many medicines already carry their own alcohol warnings. Often the biggest risk on this page is not supplement plus alcohol, but supplement plus medicine plus alcohol.
4. **Nutrient loss from drinking.** Regular heavy drinking reduces how well you absorb and store several nutrients, especially thiamine (vitamin B1), folate, magnesium, and zinc. Here supplements can help close a gap, though they don't undo the damage that drinking causes.

Keep these four mechanisms in mind as you read the table. Almost every concern below fits into one of them.

Two things the table can't show. First, **dose matters**. A standard dose of a supplement with one drink is a very different situation from a high-dose product and a heavy night. Second, **your medications matter more than anything on this list**. If you take a prescription drug, the safest move is to bring the bottle of your supplement to your pharmacist and ask.

## Sedating Herbs and Sleep Supplements

This is the group where the alcohol interaction itself is most direct. Alcohol makes you drowsy and slows your reactions. So do these supplements, to different degrees. Taken together, the effects can add up.

### Kava

Kava is the one we'd put at the top of the "don't mix" list. It's a Pacific Island root traditionally drunk for relaxation, and it acts on the brain's calming systems in a way that overlaps with alcohol. In 2002 the FDA issued a consumer advisory about rare but serious liver injury linked to kava-containing products, and several countries restricted its sale at the time. The causes are still debated, and may involve the type of extract and plant parts used, but alcohol is also hard on the liver, which is why combining them is a poor bet. Kava can also increase alcohol's impairment of coordination and judgment. Our [kava and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol) covers the details, and our [kava hangover page](/never-hungover/kava-hangover) explains what people mean when they say kava leaves them groggy.

### Valerian root

Valerian is one of the most common herbal sleep aids. The evidence that it improves sleep is mixed, but it does have mild sedative effects, and labels commonly warn against combining it with alcohol or other sedatives. The main concern is additive drowsiness: more grogginess, worse coordination, and a higher chance of accidents or falls. There are also rare case reports of liver problems linked to valerian-containing products. See our [valerian root and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/valerian-root-and-alcohol).

### Melatonin

Melatonin is a hormone, not an herb, and it doesn't sedate you the way alcohol or a sleeping pill does. It mainly signals to your body that it's time for sleep. Even so, taking it after drinking can add to drowsiness, and alcohol works against melatonin's purpose: alcohol suppresses your own melatonin release and fragments sleep in the second half of the night. If you want to know why you wake at 3 a.m. after drinking, our [melatonin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) explains the mechanism.

### Ashwagandha, CBD, and other calming supplements

- **Ashwagandha** is an adaptogen often used for stress and sleep. It may have mild sedative effects, and there are case reports of liver injury linked to ashwagandha products, which has led some regulators to look at it more closely. With alcohol, the concern is mild added sedation and liver load. See [ashwagandha and alcohol](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol).
- **CBD** can cause drowsiness on its own. In clinical trials of the prescription CBD drug Epidiolex, some patients developed elevated liver enzymes, and CBD can affect the enzymes that process many medications. That makes it worth caution with alcohol, especially at high doses. See [CBD and alcohol](/never-hungover/cbd-and-alcohol).
- **L-theanine**, the calming amino acid in tea, is one of the gentler options. There's little evidence of a meaningful interaction with moderate drinking. See [L-theanine and alcohol](/never-hungover/l-theanine-and-alcohol).
- **GABA supplements** are popular for relaxation, though how much oral GABA reaches the brain is debated. Our guide to [alcohol and GABA](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-gaba) explains how alcohol acts on this system and why it matters for next-day anxiety.

### Kratom: the one to keep fully separate

Kratom isn't usually thought of as a "sleep supplement," but it's sold in the same shops. It acts on opioid receptors, and the FDA has warned against using it. Opioid-like substances and alcohol both slow breathing, and the combination is dangerous. Don't mix kratom with alcohol. If someone has used both and is very hard to wake, has slow or shallow breathing, or has blue lips, call 911.

### The practical rule for sedating supplements

If you use any of these for sleep, skip them on nights you drink. Alcohol is already a sedative, and it will make you feel sleepy without giving you good sleep. Our guides to [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) and [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explain better options for the night after.

## Serotonin-Adjacent Supplements

These supplements act on serotonin, the brain chemical involved in mood, sleep, and many other functions. Their interaction with alcohol on its own is mostly about mood and drowsiness. The more serious risk comes when they're combined with prescription medicines that also raise serotonin.

### Why serotonin supplements need care

Too much serotonin activity can cause **serotonin syndrome**, a potentially serious reaction. Signs include agitation, confusion, a fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, sweating, shivering, muscle twitching or stiffness, and fever. It usually happens when two or more serotonin-raising substances are combined. Prescription drugs that raise serotonin include SSRIs (such as sertraline and escitalopram), SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, some migraine drugs called triptans, and others. If you take any of these, talk to your prescriber before adding a serotonin supplement. Our guides to [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol), [Zoloft and alcohol](/never-hungover/zoloft-and-alcohol), and [Lexapro and alcohol](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol) cover the medication side.

Alcohol fits into this picture in a different way. It's a depressant that can worsen low mood and anxiety, especially the next day. So if you're taking a supplement because your mood is low, drinking can work against the very thing you're trying to fix.

### St. John's wort

St. John's wort is the most important supplement on this page for drug interactions. It speeds up liver enzymes (especially CYP3A4) and a transporter called P-glycoprotein that move many drugs out of the body. According to the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, it can make a long list of medicines less effective, including birth control pills, the blood thinner warfarin, some heart and HIV medicines, and drugs that prevent organ transplant rejection. It can also cause serotonin syndrome when combined with antidepressants.

With alcohol alone, the main concerns are added dizziness and drowsiness, and the fact that alcohol can worsen the depression St. John's wort is often taken for. But if you take any prescription medicine, the bigger question is whether you should be taking St. John's wort at all. That's a conversation for your doctor or pharmacist.

### 5-HTP

5-HTP is a building block your body uses to make serotonin. Taken with antidepressants or other serotonin-raising drugs, it can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome. On its own with moderate alcohol, the main issues are added drowsiness and the mood effects of drinking. Our [5-HTP and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/5-htp-and-alcohol) goes deeper, including whether it helps with "hangxiety."

### SAM-e

SAM-e is used for mood and joint health, and it's also studied for liver health. Like 5-HTP, it can add to the effects of serotonin-raising medications. With moderate alcohol alone, there's no well-established dangerous interaction. See [SAM-e and alcohol](/never-hungover/sam-e-and-alcohol).

### Lithium orotate and mood supplements

Lithium is a prescription mood stabilizer, but low-dose lithium orotate is also sold as a supplement. Alcohol affects hydration, and lithium levels are sensitive to fluid balance. If you're considering it, our [lithium orotate and alcohol page](/never-hungover/lithium-orotate-and-alcohol) and [lithium and alcohol page](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) explain why this one needs a doctor's input.

## Liver-Load Supplements

Your liver handles almost everything you swallow, including alcohol and supplements. Most supplements are processed without trouble. A handful have been linked to liver injury in case reports, and the National Institutes of Health keeps a database called LiverTox that tracks these reports for supplements and drugs. A link in case reports doesn't mean a supplement is dangerous for everyone. These reactions are usually rare and hard to predict. But if you drink heavily or have liver disease, it makes sense to avoid stacking risks.

### Kava and your liver

Covered above. It belongs in both the sedation and liver groups, which is why it's the strongest "don't combine" on this page.

### Niacin (vitamin B3) at high doses

At normal multivitamin amounts, niacin is fine. At the high doses used for cholesterol, it's a different story. High-dose niacin causes flushing, which alcohol can make worse, and prescription niacin labels advise avoiding alcohol and hot drinks around the time of a dose for that reason. Sustained-release forms have been linked to liver toxicity at high doses. If you take high-dose niacin, talk to your doctor about alcohol. See our [niacin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/niacin-and-alcohol).

### Green tea extract

Drinking green tea is fine. Concentrated green tea extract, often sold in weight-loss supplements, is one of the more common supplement causes of liver injury in case reports, and the risk seems higher when taken on an empty stomach. If you drink heavily, it's one to avoid or discuss with your doctor.

### Turmeric and curcumin

Turmeric used in cooking is not a concern. There are case reports of liver injury linked to turmeric and curcumin supplements, often involving high-absorption formulas, such as those with added black pepper extract (piperine). For most people the risk is low, but it's another reason not to stack concentrated products if your liver is already working hard. See [turmeric and alcohol](/never-hungover/turmeric-and-alcohol).

### Vitamin A at high doses

Too much preformed vitamin A (retinol, not beta-carotene from vegetables) can damage the liver. Research going back decades suggests that regular heavy drinking makes the liver more vulnerable to vitamin A toxicity. Normal multivitamin amounts are fine, but high-dose vitamin A supplements are a poor choice for heavy drinkers.

### Iron

Alcohol increases how much iron your gut absorbs, and iron overload is hard on the liver. That matters most for people with hemochromatosis, a genetic condition that causes iron to build up, and for heavy drinkers. Don't take iron supplements unless a blood test shows you need them. See [iron and alcohol](/never-hungover/iron-and-alcohol).

### What about liver-support supplements?

On the other side are supplements marketed to protect the liver: milk thistle, NAC, TUDCA, and DHM. The honest view is that they're generally well tolerated, but none has strong human evidence that it protects against alcohol damage in people who keep drinking. There's no good evidence that any of them cancels out the effects of heavy drinking. We cover each one:

- **Milk thistle** is the most-studied liver botanical, with mixed human results. See [milk thistle and alcohol](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol).
- **NAC** provides building blocks for glutathione, one of the liver's main antioxidants. As an IV hospital treatment it's the antidote for acetaminophen overdose, but a daily pill is not a substitute for emergency care. See [NAC and alcohol](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol) and our comparison of [NAC vs milk thistle](/never-hungover/nac-vs-milk-thistle).
- **TUDCA** is a bile acid studied for liver and bile flow. See [TUDCA and alcohol](/never-hungover/tudca-and-alcohol).

For a ranking with the evidence for each, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## Blood Sugar and Bleeding Supplements

A smaller group of supplements causes trouble not through sedation or the liver, but by adding to effects alcohol already has on blood sugar or clotting.

### Berberine and ginseng (blood sugar)

Alcohol can lower blood sugar, especially when you drink without eating, because the liver is busy processing alcohol and makes less glucose. Berberine lowers blood sugar too, and it also affects how some drugs are processed. Ginseng may also lower blood sugar. The risk is highest for people taking diabetes medicines such as insulin or sulfonylureas, where low blood sugar can be dangerous and can look a lot like being drunk. If you have diabetes, talk to your doctor before combining these with alcohol. See [berberine and alcohol](/never-hungover/berberine-and-alcohol), [ginseng and alcohol](/never-hungover/ginseng-and-alcohol), and [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol).

### Ginkgo, fish oil, and other "blood-thinning" supplements

Ginkgo, high-dose fish oil, garlic supplements, and high-dose vitamin E have all been discussed as possibly adding to bleeding risk, though the evidence for most is limited. Heavy drinking also affects clotting and can interact with blood thinners like warfarin. The concern is highest if you take a blood thinner, have a bleeding disorder, or have surgery coming up. See [ginkgo biloba and alcohol](/never-hungover/ginkgo-biloba-and-alcohol), [warfarin and alcohol](/never-hungover/warfarin-and-alcohol), and [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol).

## Vitamins and Minerals Alcohol Depletes

This group is the good news. Common vitamins and minerals don't have harmful interactions with alcohol at normal doses. And for people who drink regularly, some of them can help make up for what alcohol takes away.

Heavy drinking affects nutrition in several ways. It can replace food, irritate the gut so you absorb less, increase how much you lose in urine, and change how the liver stores and activates vitamins. The nutrients most often low in heavy drinkers include:

- **Thiamine (vitamin B1).** This is the most important one. Severe thiamine deficiency can cause Wernicke's encephalopathy, a serious brain condition, and doctors routinely give thiamine to people who drink heavily. See [thiamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/thiamine-and-alcohol).
- **Folate.** Alcohol interferes with folate absorption and use. See [folic acid and alcohol](/never-hungover/folic-acid-and-alcohol).
- **Vitamin B12.** Long-term heavy drinking can affect B12 absorption. See [vitamin B12 and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol).
- **Magnesium.** Alcohol increases how much magnesium you lose in urine, and low magnesium is common in heavy drinkers. Magnesium has a low interaction risk with alcohol, but it can interfere with absorption of some antibiotics and thyroid medicine, so take those at different times. See [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) and our comparison of [magnesium glycinate vs citrate for hangovers](/never-hungover/magnesium-hangover-hangxiety-glycinate-vs-citrate-2026).
- **Zinc.** Alcohol increases zinc loss in urine and reduces absorption. See [zinc and alcohol](/never-hungover/zinc-and-alcohol).
- **Vitamin D.** Heavy drinking is linked to lower vitamin D levels and weaker bones. See [vitamin D and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-d-and-alcohol).
- **Vitamin C.** See [vitamin C and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-c-and-alcohol).

Our full guide to [vitamins depleted by alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamins-depleted-by-alcohol) covers which ones matter, the signs of deficiency, and food sources. A basic [multivitamin](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol) is a reasonable low-cost way to cover several at once.

Two cautions. First, supplements don't fix the underlying problem. If you're low on several nutrients because of drinking, the alcohol is still doing harm that pills can't undo. Second, more isn't better. Stick to normal doses unless your doctor recommends more, and remember that high-dose vitamin A and iron are exceptions where extra can hurt.

## Stimulants and Workout Supplements

- **Caffeine** doesn't sober you up. It can make you feel more alert while your blood alcohol stays the same, which can lead people to drink more or think they're fine to drive. The CDC warns against mixing alcohol with energy drinks for this reason. See [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol).
- **Pre-workout products** often contain large amounts of caffeine and other stimulants. The same "wide-awake drunk" concern applies.
- **Creatine** doesn't have a dangerous interaction with alcohol, but alcohol's dehydrating effect works against it. See [creatine and alcohol](/never-hungover/creatine-and-alcohol).
- **Electrolytes** are fine with alcohol and can help with rehydration. See [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol).

## The Medication Factor: Supplements Plus Prescriptions Plus Alcohol

This is the part of the picture that most supplement articles skip. Many people taking supplements also take prescription drugs. And many of those drugs already have their own alcohol warnings.

Common combinations that deserve a conversation with your doctor or pharmacist:

- **Antidepressants** plus St. John's wort, 5-HTP, or SAM-e, plus alcohol.
- **Sleep medicines or anxiety medicines** (such as zolpidem or benzodiazepines) plus sedating herbs, plus alcohol. All three slow the brain, and this stack can be dangerous. See [Ambien and alcohol](/never-hungover/ambien-and-alcohol) and [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol).
- **Blood thinners** plus ginkgo, fish oil, or turmeric, plus alcohol.
- **Diabetes medicines** plus berberine or ginseng, plus alcohol.
- **Birth control, heart, transplant, or HIV medicines** plus St. John's wort, which can make them stop working regardless of alcohol.
- **Gabapentin** plus sedating herbs and alcohol. See [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).

The simplest way to stay safe is to keep one list of everything you take, prescription and otherwise, and show it to your pharmacist. They can check interactions in a few minutes. For a broader overview, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Where DHM Fits In

Since this is a DHM site, it's fair to explain where DHM (dihydromyricetin) sits in this table. DHM is a flavonoid from the Japanese raisin tree, studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. A widely cited 2012 rat study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found that DHM counteracted some of alcohol's effects on GABA receptors in the brain. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited data in humans. It's promising, not proven.

In terms of safety, DHM has been generally well tolerated in the studies available, and it isn't known for the sedation or liver injury concerns that kava and some other supplements have. But there's limited data on how it interacts with prescription drugs, so if you take medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first. And DHM does not make it safe to drink more, drive, or combine alcohol with sedatives.

If you want to try it, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients, and the budget-friendly single-ingredient [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, our [DHM safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-safety-complete-guide-2025) covers side effects, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## A Simple Checklist Before You Mix

Before you take a supplement on a day you drink, run through these questions:

1. **Does it make me drowsy?** If yes, skip it on drinking nights.
2. **Do I take any prescription medicine?** If yes, ask your pharmacist about the supplement first, then about alcohol.
3. **Is it a high-dose or concentrated product?** Extracts and high-dose vitamins carry more risk than food-level amounts.
4. **Does it have a liver-injury history?** Kava, high-dose niacin, green tea extract, and some turmeric and ashwagandha products do. Avoid stacking them with heavy drinking.
5. **Am I drinking heavily or regularly?** If yes, the safest choice is to talk to your doctor before starting new supplements, and to treat any supplement as a minor factor compared with how much you drink.

If you're thinking about changing your drinking habits, that's a separate conversation worth having with a doctor. This guide is about supplement safety, not a plan for cutting back.

## The Bottom Line

- Most everyday vitamins and minerals are low-risk with moderate drinking, and some help fill gaps that heavy drinking creates.
- **Sedating herbs and sleep supplements** add to alcohol's drowsiness. Skip them on drinking nights. Kava and kratom are the strongest "don't combine."
- **Serotonin-adjacent supplements** matter most because of the antidepressants and other medicines people take alongside them. St. John's wort affects a long list of drugs.
- **Liver-load supplements** like kava, high-dose niacin, green tea extract, and high-dose vitamin A are a poor match for heavy drinking.
- **Berberine and ginkgo** need care if you take diabetes medicines or blood thinners.
- If you take any prescription medicine, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining supplements and alcohol.

Two more guides are worth knowing. If you take St. John's wort for mood, our [St. John's wort and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/st-johns-wort-and-alcohol) covers why it needs extra care alongside drinking and other medicines. And for prescription and over-the-counter drugs rather than supplements, our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) summarizes how the main drug classes interact with alcohol.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Which supplements should you never mix with alcohol?**

Kava and kratom are the clearest "don't combine" cases. Kava adds to alcohol's sedation and has been linked to rare but serious liver injury, and kratom acts on opioid receptors, which together with alcohol can dangerously slow breathing. Other sedating herbs like valerian are best skipped on drinking nights. If you take prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before combining any supplement with alcohol.

**Is it safe to take vitamins after drinking alcohol?**

For most people, yes. Common vitamins and minerals like a multivitamin, B vitamins, vitamin C, vitamin D, magnesium, and zinc don't have harmful interactions with alcohol at normal doses. Heavy drinking can actually deplete several of them, especially thiamine, folate, magnesium, and zinc. The exceptions are high-dose vitamin A, high-dose niacin, and iron, which can be harder on the liver in heavy drinkers.

**Can I take melatonin or valerian after drinking?**

It's best not to. Both can add to alcohol's drowsiness, and alcohol already disrupts sleep in the second half of the night, so the combination tends to give you grogginess without better sleep. If you take a prescription sleep or anxiety medicine as well, the combination can be more dangerous, so talk to your doctor before mixing any of them with alcohol.

**Does St. John's wort interact with alcohol?**

On its own with moderate alcohol, the main concerns are added dizziness and drowsiness, and alcohol can worsen the low mood St. John's wort is often taken for. The bigger issue is that St. John's wort speeds up the breakdown of many prescription drugs, including birth control pills, warfarin, and some heart and HIV medicines, and it can cause serotonin syndrome with antidepressants. If you take any medication, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using it.

**Can supplements protect my liver from alcohol?**

There's no good evidence that any supplement cancels out the effects of heavy drinking. Milk thistle, NAC, TUDCA, and DHM are generally well tolerated and have some research behind them, mostly from lab and animal studies with limited human data. The most reliable way to protect your liver is to drink less. If you drink heavily or have liver disease, talk to your doctor before starting any supplement.

**Is it safe to take 5-HTP and alcohol together?**

For someone not on medication, the main concerns with moderate drinking are added drowsiness and the mood effects of alcohol. The real risk is combining 5-HTP with antidepressants, tramadol, triptans, or other drugs that raise serotonin, which can lead to serotonin syndrome. If you take any of these, talk to your prescriber before using 5-HTP.

**Should I take magnesium before or after drinking?**

Magnesium has a low interaction risk with alcohol, and drinking increases how much magnesium you lose in urine, so many people take it in the evening or the next day. It can cause loose stools at higher doses, especially the citrate and oxide forms. Magnesium can also interfere with the absorption of some antibiotics and thyroid medicine, so take those at different times and check with your pharmacist if you're unsure.
